title: Taylor / Maclaurin series
subject: Maths AA HL
hard_bit: You can compute the coefficients, but it is not obvious why adding terms helps, or why the approximation collapses far from the centre.
shows: The polynomial is built up one term at a time against sin(x). Each new term grips the curve over a wider interval, and outside that interval it shoots off to infinity - which is what radius of convergence means, visually.
try_changing: `FUNCTION` - one line: `"sin(x)"`, `"cos(x)"`, `"e^x"` or `"ln(1+x)"`. The last one has radius of convergence 1 (it converges for -1 < x <= 1); the shaded band shows where, and past x = 1 more terms make things worse.
`MAX_TERMS` - how many non-zero terms to build up to.
Add your own entry to `SERIES`, e.g. the geometric series 1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x² + ... (`term=lambda k: (1, k)`, `radius=1`).

equations.caption: Maclaurin series: a Taylor series centred on x = 0
Only odd powers appear, so n non-zero terms reach x to the power 2n - 1
Radius of convergence 1: no number of terms works beyond x = 1

questions.q: With sin(x) selected, will the 10-term polynomial stay within 0.05 of the curve for a whole wave either side of 0 (out to x = 2π ≈ 6.3)? Predict, then drag Terms to 10.
questions.a: Yes, and a bit more: the readout says it tracks sin(x) from about x = -7.5 to 7.5. The series for sin(x) converges for every x, so each extra term pushes that edge further out; with 5 terms the edge is only at about 3.7.

questions.q: Select ln(1+x). At x = 2, does going from 5 terms to 10 terms bring the polynomial closer to the curve, or send it further away?
questions.a: Further away. At x = 2 the 5-term polynomial gives about 5.1 and the 10-term one about -64.8, against ln 3 ≈ 1.1. x = 2 is outside the radius of convergence (1), where the terms 2ⁿ/n grow instead of shrinking, so every term added makes it worse. Inside the shaded band the opposite happens: with 10 terms the readout's good region reaches x = 1.

title: Projectile motion with air resistance
subject: Physics HL
hard_bit: Exam questions use the vacuum parabola, so it is easy to believe 45 degrees is always optimal and that the path is symmetric. Neither survives contact with drag, and there is no neat formula to show why.
shows: Real trajectories against the vacuum parabola, and range plotted against launch angle. The optimum slides below 45 degrees, and the faster you launch, the further it slides.
try_changing: `speed` in `main()` - push it to 80 m/s and watch the optimum drop from 40 to 35 degrees.
`DRAG_K` - set it to 0 to recover the textbook result: the best angle is 45 degrees, and the range matches v² sin 2θ / g to within one step.
`MASS` - a ping-pong ball vs a cannonball at the same speed.
`DT` - make it 0.05 and compare with the exact vacuum range. Big steps drift, which is why step size matters in any numerical method.

equations.caption: Drag of size kv², always pointing against the velocity

equations.tex: \vec v_{n+1} = \vec v_n + \vec a(\vec v_n)\,\Delta t, \qquad \vec x_{n+1} = \vec x_n + \vec v_{n+1}\,\Delta t
equations.caption: Semi-implicit Euler: update the velocity first, then move with the new velocity
The no-drag range the dashed curve reproduces, greatest at 45°

questions.q: At the default drag (k = 0.0013), what happens to the best angle if you double the launch speed from 40 m/s to 80 m/s?
questions.a: It drops, from 40° to 35° (press 'Jump to best angle' at each speed). Drag grows as v², so at 80 m/s it is a much bigger force compared with the weight, and every second in the air costs more range. A lower, flatter launch spends less time in the air and keeps more of its horizontal speed. In a vacuum the best angle stays at 45° at both speeds.

questions.q: With drag on, is the path still symmetric - does the ball come down at the same angle it went up?
questions.a: No. Watch the solid curve against the dashed vacuum parabola: with drag the ball comes down more steeply than it went up, and its highest point is more than halfway along the range. Drag keeps removing horizontal speed, so the second half of the flight covers less ground than the first. Set k to 0 and the two curves coincide again.

title: Maxwell-Boltzmann and activation energy
subject: Chemistry HL
hard_bit: The curve is usually drawn once, so 'a 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate' stays a memorised fact rather than something you can see.
shows: Raising the temperature barely moves the peak - it stretches the tail past Ea. Drag the temperature slider and watch the shaded area multiply while the curve itself hardly shifts.
try_changing: `EA_KJ` - a higher barrier makes the temperature sensitivity much stronger: at 80 kJ/mol a 10 K rise multiplies the fraction past Ea by 2.77, at 25 kJ/mol only by 1.36. This is the same reason catalysts (lower Ea) work.
`MASS` - compare hydrogen (0.002 / N_A) against nitrogen at the same temperature. The speed curve changes completely; the energy curve and the fraction past Ea do not change at all.

equations.caption: Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution, a fraction of molecules per unit energy; the mass cancels
The exact shaded area past Ea

questions.q: With Ea = 50 kJ/mol, does raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K really double the fraction of molecules that can react?
questions.a: Nearly: set 300 K and the readout says another 10 K multiplies the fraction by 1.88 (the Arrhenius factor alone gives 1.91). 'Doubles per 10 K' is a rule of thumb for barriers near 50 kJ/mol at room temperature; drop Ea to 25 kJ/mol and the same 10 K gives only 1.36×.

questions.q: Heat the gas from 300 K to 600 K. Does the peak of the energy curve move anywhere near Ea = 50 kJ/mol?
questions.a: No. The peak sits at RT/2, which only moves from about 1.2 to 2.5 kJ/mol - switch off the log scale to see it barely shift. Yet the shaded fraction past Ea rises from 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ to 1.7 × 10⁻⁴, about 16,000 times more. Temperature works by stretching the tail, not by moving the whole curve past the barrier.

title: Electron orbitals — shapes, fill order, metals
subject: Chemistry HL
hard_bit: Linking orbital pictures to a written configuration — especially once the d-block starts, and Cr / Cu refuse the naive Aufbau answer.
shows: Interactive walkthrough: s/px/py/pz shapes, two electrons per orbital, periodic-table blocks with the diagonal fill order (4s before 3d), then Fe vs Cr/Cu exceptions.
try_changing: In section 4 of the script, swap Cr for Cu (`fill_aufbau(29)`).
Add Mn (Z = 25) - Aufbau works: `[Ar] 4s² 3d⁵`, already half-filled.
Try other ions with `ion_config`: `ion_config(25, 2)` gives Mn²⁺ as `[Ar] 3d⁵`, and `ion_config(17, -1)` gives Cl⁻ as `[Ne] 3s² 3p⁶`.

equations.caption: The most electrons a main energy level can hold

equations.tex: \text{fill order: lower } n + l \text{ first; for a tie, lower } n \qquad (s, p, d, f:\ l = 0, 1, 2, 3)
equations.caption: The Madelung rule behind the diagonal chart - it puts 4s (4 + 0) before 3d (3 + 2)
The two exceptions IB asks for: a half-filled or full 3d sublevel

questions.q: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, and 3d was filled last. When Fe forms Fe²⁺, which two electrons does it lose? Predict, then pick Fe in part 4.
questions.a: The two 4s electrons, not two 3d ones: the ions line shows Fe²⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁶ (and Fe³⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁵). 4s fills before 3d, but once 3d holds electrons the 4s electrons are the outermost, so a positive ion loses them first. [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴ is the classic wrong answer.

questions.q: Cr is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than the Aufbau guess 4s² 3d⁴. How many unpaired electrons does each arrangement have?
questions.a: 4 for the Aufbau guess and 6 for the real one - the two Cr panels count them. Moving one electron from 4s into the empty 3d orbital gives a half-filled 3d sublevel with every electron unpaired and parallel (Hund). Half-filled and full d sublevels are especially stable, and 4s and 3d are close in energy, so the move lowers the energy.
